Meta Tags Explained

What Are Meta Tags & Why Do They Matter?

Meta tags are HTML snippets in your page head that tell search engines and social platforms what your page is about.

Title tag

The most important on-page SEO element. Appears as the clickable blue link in Google results. Keep it 50–60 characters and include your primary keyword near the start.

Meta description

The grey text under your title in Google results. Keeps it 120–160 characters with a clear benefit and call to action. Does not directly affect rankings but massively affects click-through rate.

Open Graph tags

Control how your page looks on Facebook, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. Without OG tags social platforms guess — and usually get it wrong. Add an og:image for dramatically higher engagement.

Twitter / X cards

Twitter uses its own card system separate from Open Graph. The summary_large_image card shows a big image above your tweet — much more engaging than a plain text link.

Robots meta tag

Tells search crawlers what to do with the page. Use noindex for thank-you pages, staging sites, or admin pages you do not want appearing in search results.

SEO best practices

Every page needs a unique title and description. Include your target keyword naturally in the title. Write descriptions that compel clicks and update OG tags whenever you share content.

FAQ

Meta Tag Questions Answered

Do meta keywords still matter for SEO?+

No. Google stopped using the meta keywords tag in 2009. Bing and most other search engines also ignore it. You can include keywords for internal tracking purposes but it has no effect on rankings.

How long should my meta description be?+

Google typically displays 120–160 characters. Longer descriptions get cut off with dots. Write the most important information first. Google may also rewrite your description if it thinks something else on the page is more relevant to the search query.

What size should my OG image be?+

The recommended size is 1200×630 pixels. This displays correctly on Facebook, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. Keep file size under 1MB for fast loading.

Why is Google showing a different description than mine?+

Google may rewrite your meta description if it determines that content from the page itself better answers the search query. This is normal. Focus on making your page content strong — Google will usually use your description for branded searches.

Can I use the same meta description on multiple pages?+

Technically yes, but you should not. Duplicate meta descriptions are a missed opportunity. Each page should have a unique description that accurately describes that specific page's content.
